newsitem.title: USA: Texas "tight gas" exemption saved in budget battle.
newsitem.headline: Texas "tight gas" exemption saved in budget battle.

text.p: A legislative proposal to repeal a state tax exemption for natural gas produced from tight geological formations has been taken off the table for now, Texas Railroad Commission Chairman Charles Matthews said on Wednesday.

The so-called "tight gas" exemption, worth an estimated $144 million a year to Texas producers, had been threatened as legislators in Austin consider a sweeping overhaul of the state's property tax structure in their biennial session.
"I am very concerned about us losing our tight-gas exemption," Matthews said. "It's temporarily off the table, but I don't think anybody knows how it's going to play out."

Industry lobbyists are swarming the halls of the Texas Capitol in Austin seeking to avoid possible tax hikes ranging from adoption of a state tax on aviation fuel to repeal of existing agricultural tax exemptions.
The oil and gas industry benefits from a total $184 million in annual tax exemptions, mainly for production from wells that otherwise could not be produced economically, he said.
One proposal, to eliminate a tax break on lignite mining in the state, threatens to make lignite mines uncompetitive in Texas, the nation's fifth largest coal producing state, Matthews said.
"I think the lignite is so marginal that the tax could very well close those mines," he said. "Texas lignite (mining) in most areas is just holding on."
